utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today is Monday, 22nd of June, 2009. First of all, good afternoon to you, Mr. Praljak, and to you, Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic, and to Mr. Stojic. Good afternoon to the accused who are not present for various reasons. And my greetings to the Defence counsel and to the counsel who are not in court today. Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer and all the representatives of the OTP, together with their associates. Good afternoon to all the people assisting us. First of all, I'll give the floor to the Registrar, who has a few IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the list submitted by the Prosecution entitled "Prosecution Objections to Documents Tendered through Slobodan Praljak by Praljak Defence" will be Exhibit IC1030.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Trial Chamber has two short decisions to hand down; first of all, regarding the incidents in interpretation on the 18th of June, 2009. Further to the Accused Praljak's observation during the hearing of the 18th of June, 2009, the Trial Chamber instructed the Registry to launch an immediate inquiry into the allegedly offensive remarks by an interpreter during the hearing. On the 19th of June, 2009, Mr. Kovacic sent an e-mail to the Trial Chamber's legal officer in which he made clear that three of his colleagues, who had been listening to the B/C/S booth during the hearing, had told him that the interpreter at issue had not made any offensive remarks. In Mr. Kovacic's view, an inquiry into the incident was, therefore, no longer necessary. Based on the above information, the Trial Chamber concludes that there is no reason for further inquiry into the matter. However, the Trial Chamber reminds all interpreters that they are not to make any personal comments in the booth when their mikes are on. Second oral ruling, which is much longer, it may be complex; therefore, I'll be slow. Oral ruling to clarify the filing of IC lists. At the hearing of the 15th of June, 2009, the Prosecution asked the Chamber for a seven-day dead-line to be given as of the time the latest IC list of the Praljak Defence was filed in order to file their objections. On that same day, the Trial Chamber granted the motion. Proprio motu, the Trial Chamber has decided to make further observations with regarding filings of IC list objections and answers. The Praljak Defence, during examination-in-chief of the Accused Praljak, filed several IC lists. The Prosecution was to file objections, if any, to such IC lists on the day. The Trial Chamber understands that this method enables parties to best prepare for the rest of their testimony by the Accused Praljak. However, the Trial Chamber reminds parties that in keeping with the Trial Chamber's oral decisions of the 18th of May, 2009, and further to directive or guide-line number 8, a final decision on the admission of exhibits will only take place once the testimony by Accused Praljak is over. In order to be able to reach a decision, the Trial Chamber instructs all parties to file, on the day after the testimony of Accused Praljak has been completed, their consolidated IC lists for exhibits to be admitted. With regard to the Praljak Defence, their IC lists may include IC lists filed during the testimony of the accused. The Praljak Defence could also file a different list, but then the onus is on the Praljak Defence to point it out to the Trial Chamber. The same will apply to the Prosecution, should they, during their cross-examination, file IC lists for admission of exhibits. The other parties to the proceedings will be able to file their IC lists, seeking admission of exhibits, once the testimony by Accused Praljak has been completed. When the testimony has been completed, and on the day following the filing of all IC lists seeking exhibits to be admitted, the parties will be able to file their objections. The Prosecution will file a new IC list, including their objections, if any, against IC lists filed by all parties to the proceedings. This IC list will include the objections filed during the testimony of the Accused Praljak, or the list could be different, with the obligation then for the Prosecution to point the difference to the Trial Chamber. IC lists, including responses to objections, can be filed on the day following filing of IC lists with objections. Very well. Read it again once it has all settled down. It may seem difficult at first blush, but it is quite simple. And once you have read it all, you will understand that it is very simple, indeed. Once Mr. Praljak has completed his testimony, there will be new IC lists that will become the final lists and that may include the same lists or slightly modified lists. But if there is any modification, it must be pointed out to the Chamber. So read it quite at ease. Otherwise, we're going to go into endless discussions. The Trial Chamber was of the view that it was necessary to clarify all this by way of a decision so that you understand that actually you can have an IC list that would be filed, say, today, there might be objections by the Prosecution, and then in the end, when Mr. Praljak finishes in July, there would be a new IC list which would be, as it were, a consolidated IC list. You seem to have some doubts, Mr. Stringer. I mean, you will have this in your own language, and then if it still worries you, well, just ask the legal officer and she will give you all the necessary explanations in tete-a-tete, as it were. So we're going to continue with the presidential transcripts. Remember, we ended with them last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar -- we have a new Registrar today in court. I hope she will be able to keep up. Please call up P414, and more specifically page 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everyone in the court. I apologise for intervening. If I may have a minute, while we are looking for the document. Your Honours, I would like to express my concern with regard to the dynamics envisaged in your ruling that you have just read. General Praljak's Defence, in theory, will have, at the end, probably expressed their opposition vis-a-vis the total of six lists. We don't know if everyone else is going to submit something, but we shall, at any rate, have to go through all the IC lists of the Defence teams and the Prosecution in a single day and put forth our objections. We may be in a slightly more inconvenient position than the other parties involved. Therefore, I would kindly ask, if necessary, to give us, in advance, some reasonable period of time for us to review all the six lists, but working on the assumption that at least the Prosecution list is going to be a long one. And that will be a little bit difficult to finalise in one day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We take due note of your request. The Trial Chamber will discuss this, and we will hand down an oral ruling on the matter. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I simply wanted to join in the concern or the reservations expressed by my friend Mr. Kovacic. If I was looking tentative earlier, it was only because of concern that the requirement that other parties file their responses one day after the IC lists are initially filed, that was the concern I had. Our IC list that we filed today contained responses to about 240 documents, and it takes a long time to go through the transcript and see what was said and determine whether an objection is warranted or not. And I don't know how many exhibits the other Defence teams might be intending to offer on the basis of their own cross-examinations. But the only concern that I had, and I think it's one shared by Mr. Kovacic, is that it may be necessary for one or more of the parties to ask for more time to file their responses or objections once we've got the lists filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll take this on board as well, and you will have a decision that will satisfy everybody, I promise you. Mr. Praljak, we have a presidential transcript of the 29th of August, 1992. The meeting had started at 6.00 p.m., ended at 7.20, with Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Boban, Mr. Manolic, and Mr. Susak. You were not there. And at the meeting, as you can see, that's towards the beginning of the text, Mr. Tudjman said that the seat towns of Nevesinje and Gacko had no reason to be included in the Croat region, but the problem was for the Bosnian Croat Posavina. What did Mr. Tudjman mean, exactly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to say that within the scope of this internal division of regions, or entities, or any kind of internal structuring of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Posavina or, rather, in some of its municipalities, the Croats constituted a majority. I am aware of this transcript, because this took place after the London Conference, and there's another attempt to see what kind of internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to look. Gacko and Nevesinje were populated by the Serbs, and after all, one needed to hear what their view was about the state structure. There was also mention of the embargo, because Croatia was under pressure not to provide any weapons to the HVO, and there was a proposal for a sort of Muslim Croatian state within Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there were always some ideas being put forward in order to find out what the internal structure was going to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have document P466, page 54. P466.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One more note, Your Honours. In this document 414, Mr. Mate Boban explicitly and clearly proposed a joint command of the BH Army and HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have an opportunity to return to the topic of joint command. So we were going to have a look at page 54. Let me check that it is now on the screen. Yes, it is. This is a meeting held on the 11th of September, 1992, with Mr. Susak, with you, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Agotic, Mr. Lukic, and Mr. Radic, together with Mr. Tudjman. The latter said that Croatia will insist on the fact that the regions that were part of the Croatian Banovina were, demographically and geopolitically, part of Croatia. So this is what he said. Now, how do you understand his reference to those Banovina areas which, as he seems to say, were demographically and geopolitically part of Croatia? And you attended the meeting, so you must have heard him say that. How are we to understand his words?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very clearly, Your Honours, in what used to be the Croatian Banovina, in the demographic sense, the Croatian population constituted a majority. Now, when you are preparing an internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he had in mind that it should be taken into account that this territory, this space, these municipalities, call it what you will, populated demographically by the majority of Croats, that it should represent within Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, actually, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be organized in such a way that the people living down there and constitute a majority enjoy equal rights as the other two peoples. He said that they used to be -- he's talking in past tense. They used to be part of geopolitical Croatia. Of course, there was a geopolitical and national interest of the Republic of Croatia. It is not a small matter for Croatia to have the Croats expelled from the Neretva Valley and Herzegovina, Central Bosnia and other parts, and then, especially in war time, you have the JNA coming or the VRS coming to the borders, or even the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is unjust and illogical and should be a matter of interest. So he is talking in past tense, and he's talking about the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Initially, I hadn't planned to ask you the following question, but I have to do now. Look at what Mr. Tudjman said also in the third paragraph. He mentioned their wish to create an Islamist state. You mentioned the issue several times, and so does Mr. Tudjman here. In September 1992, was the emergence of an Islamic state a cause for such risks that all authorities had the topic in mind? Is that the reason why Mr. Tudjman mentioned the issue here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours. The SDA was made up of people who had been in jail as Young Muslims in the past. You know, when people who are over 40 or over 50 years old had been imprisoned for their ideas, then one cannot ever assume that they would abandon their ideas and that they would come up with a political platform that they had never revoked or invoked, and that is the Islamic platform. And if you have this kind of concern prevailing in the international community as well, then you might say that there was a real concern there. And in the last paragraph, Tudjman is talking here about our, meaning Croatian, engagement should be of such nature only to the extent to ensure that we keep the Croats there and not worsen their position; whereas, on the other hand, we are totally prepared to become disengaged in providing support to the Muslims and Croats only when everybody, the Serbs and the Muslims and everybody else, is forced to cease all military operations. And that was his hope throughout the whole time in the aftermath of all these conferences, hoping that somebody from the international community would come up with a stronger view, and instruction, and how to carry out all the propositions from Cutileiro onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to a document in which there are several relevant pages. It is P00498, page 67 to start with. This is a meeting that took place in Zagreb on the 17th of September, 1992, chaired by President Tudjman. We have HDZ of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who attend the meeting. Page 71, at the very top of the page, apparently Mr. Tudjman said that the problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina has a historic and geopolitical dimension for the Croatian people. The preamble of the Croatian Constitution said that preserving the state entailed that the Croatian Banovina had to be materialised. Mr. Praljak, you remember the Constitution. It recalled the issue of the Croatian Banovina. On page 67, Mr. Tudjman recalled that. Apparently, you didn't attend the meeting, but to the best of your recollection of the time, was the issue of the Croatian Banovina so important, constitutionally, that it caused discussions within the Croatian society?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the preamble to the Croatian Constitution, it is stated that nearly 800 years of our personal union and other forms of union with Hungary, Austria, Turks, et cetera, as far as the Croatian Constitution is concerned, the issue of Bosnia-Herzegovina is the issue that President Tudjman was speaking about. However, Banovina was something that provided security and protection for the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the term "Banovina" was being used here as a synonym for the protection of the Croats in the places where they constitute a majority. He further went on to say that Croatia had been helping the Bosnian Croats and that, thanks to that, it defended and saved not only the Croats, but Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. He also added that if this part is lost to the Serbs, the same will happen, what is now happening in Republika Srpska, from where 200.000 Croats had fled and who had never -- have never returned to this day. Of course, he was much too realistic a politician, and he knew that assuming that the Serbs had captured this without us managing to defend itself, another 300.000 Croats would flee to Croatia. They would not remain living in something that would be called Yugoslavia. So it is quite clear that we are talking here about Bosnia-Herzegovina, we are talking about the interests of the Croatian people and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that the assistance was provided to both the Croats and the BH Army in order to fend off the Serbs. Even more was received by the BH Army, not only from us but from other sources as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 69. That might shed light on what you have just said. Page 69, third paragraph, beginning with the following words: "In other words ..." President Tudjman thus said that Croatia had defended Herzegovina with the HVO so that they could establish a Croatian government there, and he expresses his intention to maintain -- to keep the government. And then he calls on all to work towards military unity and political power. In saying so, through the words that we see here, it seems that Mr. Tudjman is in favour of a Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with a role to be played by the HVO. And since there is already a government there, Mr. Tudjman seems to be in favour of it. This is the third paragraph. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that this also attests to the same identical story, and that is, first of all, Franjo Tudjman is aware already, as a general from World War II, of how Tito duped Churchill, and in places where you are defeated, nobody from the international community is going to help you go back or impose a just solution. So where you are, you need to defend yourself. Secondly, to maintain the Croatian authority in the area which we had defended ourselves in is exactly what the HVO put in its documents; that all the institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina are recognised as long as they do not wish to join Yugoslavia. The HD-HZ [as interpreted] will stop as soon as an internal solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina is found. You saw that in the document by Mr. Jaganjac, and as I said, there is no HZ-HB; there's only the Vance-Owen Plan, if the Muslims accept the Vance-Owen Plan. And then in the last paragraph, you see where it clearly says the Muslims want war. And then he repeats, We mustn't quarrel with the Muslims, we mustn't quarrel. I agree, but also we cannot submit to the fez, we must not recognise the majority. We cannot submit our policy under Alija Izetbegovic or the Serbs. So it means we would be equal in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croats are an equal people. And again he also speaks about, and I already said that, that the Muslims in refugee centres -- are in refugee centres, can be found in cafes, so there was talk that after the war with the Muslims, there would be war with the Catholics. So this accords with their desire to be in a majority in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have an important mistake in the transcript on page 12, line 8. General Praljak said, "HZ-HB will cease to exist." In the transcript, it says "HDZ would cease to exist."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's now take a look at page 70. At first, I didn't intend to ask you any questions on this, but when I was looking at the transcript earlier this morning, I thought that this was very important. Mr. Tudjman is talking about the Mujahedins. He mentions them, saying that they might be 1.100 to 1300 of them, and they would come from Sudan, but also from Afghanistan and Iran. Very well. You have already developed this theory of the Mujahedins. You've developed it over -- when you were asking questions to many witnesses. And here Mr. Tudjman is confirming the fact that there are 1300 Mujahedins. Now, here's my question: When you were commanding the HVO, did the intelligence you gather make it possible for you to know that in front of you, you had the ABiH, but that within the ABiH there could have been - I'm only saying there could have been - up to 1300 foreign combatants? Of course, some of the Mujahedins might be local people, but did you know that there were these categories of people in the ABiH and that there were these 1300 combatants in front of you? Were you aware of it, as commander, because Mr. Tudjman is talking about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we were completely aware. We did have information, and on the basis of everything that I knew then, and later, I still assert that the number of Mujahedin in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the number of foreign nationals in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was above 5.000 at a certain period in time. I think at one point in time in 1993, actually in late 1993, there were more than 4.000 Mujahedin in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you showed us a video, a video I know well, where we see an exchange of prisoners. HVO soldiers are exchanged for Mujahedin, under the auspices of UNPROFOR, and this exchange occurs in Zenica. Among the prisoners exchanged, there were a few Mujahedins who had been captured by the HVO. And if I remember well, this exchange occurred in April, after Mr. Totic had been kidnapped. Now, at the time, did you get any information on the investigations on these Mujahedins? Did you know what their goals were, what -- how they had come about? Did you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had plenty of information about that. Also, we knew from which countries they were coming, their numbers, and what they did. There were several factors, acceptance by a certain part of the structure around Alija Izetbegovic and some of his officers, but there was also resistance among parts of the population, in terms of the Mujahedin, because they abused them, because, in their opinion, these people were not good Muslims because they were drinking, the women were not covering themselves, and so on and so forth. But they enjoyed covert and overt public support of Alija Izetbegovic, Dzemal Merdan, Fikret Muslimovic and so on, and we did have all of those -- we knew about all of those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to ask you a question from you, Mr. Praljak. On the same page, we find the sentence here in the second paragraph, the last sentence of it, and I quote: "They figure there are four million Turkish citizens with origins in Bosnia who are prepared, and are organising in their own way, to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina." Frankly, I am taken aback. I have never heard about it. Of course, it is not a very big thing if I did not hear about it, but I fear really that it is somehow out of proportions and, for me, it is ridiculous. I wonder -- I mean ridiculous that President Tudjman spoke about the four million Turkish civilians. As we all know, the Turkish presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina finally happened to terminate in the 19th century, in 1878 at the latest, and that is why I believe that speaking about four million Turks with early origins in Bosnia, it is somehow something which is -- which cannot be substantiated. So I wonder, what is your view about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position, Your Honour, is opposite to yours. These are facts. These are true facts that you can check still today. What occurred were two major exoduses of Muslims from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and -- well, let's say three. After the Berlin Congress in 1879, when -- 1878, when Bosnia was given to Austria to manage, and then with the annexation, Austria in a way took charge and ruled over Bosnia, as of 1908, when the Muslims who, for several centuries, especially the upper class, ruled that region, could not reconcile themselves to the fact that a significant or substantial change had occurred in the internal order of the state, so a vast number of Muslims left Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as Montenegro, Sandzak. And in particular, after World War I, after the Serbs, as the victors in World War I, were given to run Yugoslavia, the old Yugoslavia, there was another major exodus. There is a vast population in Turkey that had come from what we call the former Yugoslavia. So this figure is not exaggerated, Your Honours. I think there is publicly-available data if you're interested. I can look for the precise figure, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, if I understand you well, after the Berlin Congress there was an important exodus, a great number of Muslims who knew that Austria was about to manage the country and who decided to leave for Turkey. And after World War I, because of Serbian hegemony, there was a second exodus. So almost 90 years later, this could have resulted into four million Turks who had origins in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whose great-grandfathers were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially in 1908, there was a major one. And then after World War I, when the Serbs abolished the land rights of the Beys and the Agas, who had vast estates, when they implemented the agrarian reform, a well-known act, and they distributed the land to the serfs, to the people, so they moved from Yugoslavia, also they moved out from Macedonia, Yugoslavia, Sandzak. Muslims were leaving all of these places and going towards Turkey. It was not only that they were moving out from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's look at page 71 now, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do not want to continue the discussion, and I do not want to prevent Judge Antonetti to continue his own questioning, but I would like only to say that I am sure that these figures are exaggerated. I also know something about the former Yugoslavia, about the history of that region, from the 19th and 20th century, but, anyway, I believe this kind of figure of four million is part and parcel of the kind of the, quote/unquote "Muslim threats," and therefore I do not think that it is being substantiated by any other major source. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I asked for page 71 to be placed on the screen. Look at the last paragraph in this page, please. Tudjman is saying that during his negotiation with Izetbegovic, Izetbegovic not wanted to sign a military agreement which would have allowed the Croats to directly involve themselves in Bosanska Posavina. As far as you're concerned, could you tell us why Izetbegovic refused to sign this military agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was hoping that he would sign an agreement with the Serbs to the -- or at the expense of the Croats because they would find some sort of historical agreement. If a military agreement were to be signed with the Croats, then he would clearly opt for a choice of who was the aggressor and who was helping him, and this was not possible in the case of Mr. Izetbegovic. He wanted to sit on both chairs and be in with all the players. And as far as reaching agreements, he tried to reach an agreement with the stronger side. Had the Serbs not done what they did to them, he would have entered into an agreement with them against the Croats. In this way, he signed an agreement only on the border areas, and that prevented Croatia from sending its regular troops, because there was no military agreement, and that is how we lost Posavina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's look at page 78, then, because there might be a reason explaining why Mr. Izetbegovic did not want to sign this agreement. Page 78, first paragraph, please. Here, Tudjman said that he was in favour of an agreement that should be signed between Croatia and Bosnia that would allow Croatia to legally interfere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Don't you think that this was a reason why Mr. Izetbegovic was so reluctant? Mr. Tudjman is saying if there had been an agreement, Croatia could legally have interfered in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is what's written. What's your opinion on this, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours, but legitimate in terms of defence. If you connect that it means the defence of Posavina, that's the area where both Croats and Muslims were killed and persecuted. He's not saying that that army should go to Nevesinje and Gacko, not there where the Serbs were, but in places where the Serbs wished to expel either the Bosniaks or the Muslims. And you know, yourself, how many Bosniaks and Croats were expelled from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at document P524, page 10. This is a meeting of the National Defence Council, held on September 26. You attend -- you are attending this meeting, as well as Mr. Mesic, Lukic, Sarinic, Susak, and of course Mr. Tudjman. During this meeting, Mr. Tudjman is announcing that the political and military situation is quite difficult and that the conclusion of an agreement could justify the engagement of Croatia and Herzegovina. It seems to be, anyway. Mr. Tudjman is saying that the military situation is very difficult and that the best solution might be, after all, to reach an agreement so that Croatia could be joining forces with Bosnia-Herzegovina. You attended this meeting. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All I can add is that the same identical story goes on, and that is that Tudjman is saying perhaps the Serbs would stop firing on Jajce if the hydroelectric power-station would be given to them. Again, he says that we have to go with the Muslims in order to be able to defend our positions; that it was necessary to understand the Serbs, too. However, without resolving Bosnia and Herzegovina, the problem in Croatia itself will not be resolved; Drina up to the Baranja. Well, it's a principled and clear political position in a war. You don't wish to attack anyone, you don't wish to wage war. You want an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina where the Croatian people would be sovereign and a part of the -- and constituent element, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last sentence by Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you see that right after all this, Tudjman said that Panic said before the United Nations that, We had 30.000 regulars and 10.000 irregular Croatian soldiers. I don't know who this Panic is. I assume it must be Mr. Milosevic's ambassador.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Panic? No, at the time Panic was the president of Serbia. Milosevic was the president of Yugoslavia. Panic was a Serb who -- it's important. He was an American citizen. He had lived for 30 or 40 years in the United States. He was a businessman, and the Americans managed in some way to get him to Serbia. But, however, that man, as much as he wished to, had no clue about politics, and he had a lot of misconceptions, and he didn't really last that long. He was not really well versed in matters, but somebody told him that there were 30.000 regular troops over there, Croatian troops, so -- but, you see, what can I say? We had problems getting 10 people, never mind 30.000 people. These are figures stemming from war propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So Panic exaggerated the figures?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absurdly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at P00866 now, pages 8, 9 and 10. This is a meeting held on December 5th, 1992, with Bobetko, Susak and Tudjman. According to this document, I don't believe that you attended this meeting, Mr. Praljak. Mr. Tudjman, in these three pages, is saying the following: Croatia had secured Croatian territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the western territories that were of strategic importance to Croatia. He also says that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina benefit from complete independence in the area of HZ-HB; as well, they also benefit from international recognition, and that he was also -- he also writes to part of Bosanska Posavina. And he says that recognising the rights of the Croats in Bosanska Posavina could have been possible if the borders had been correctly drawn out, and that the strategic interest of Croatia is to make sure that the Cazin, Bihac and Krajina side of the Serbs, given the geopolitical position of Croatia. So in this meeting, Mr. Tudjman is taking stock of the situation as of December 1992, and he is saying, as far as Croatia is concerned, the western Croatian territory is of strategic importance. Do you agree with what Mr. Tudjman was saying at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In a number of presidential transcripts, we see that Mr. Tudjman is always mentioning Bosanska Posavina. Why is he always mentioning this region? He's mentioning it at all meetings all the time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because 150.000 Croats lived in that area, which is not a negligible number for a people numbering a total of 4 million. I mean, it's not a small number if we were talking about cows, never mind people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is your explanation to explain why Mr. Tudjman was so interested in this region. Let's move to another document, P01544. Now we're going to move to 1993. We would like to have page 24 on the screen, please. This is a meeting held on February 24th, 1993, National Council for Defence, a meeting held at 6.00 p.m. It lasts for an hour and a half. We have Sarinic, Marinic, Vedris, Jarnjak, Bobetko, Tus, Sanader, Sansevic [phoen], Tudjman, Pasalic, Greguric. It seems that you did not attend this meeting. However, on page 24, Tudjman seems to say that the Croats must maintain their position according to which Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain independent, but it should remain so as the union of three people, three constitutive people. It seems that Mr. Tudjman is recognising the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina and actually is not challenging it, but he seems to be calling for a union of the three constituent peoples. What is your opinion on this, please? How do you perceive what he just said?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, always in the same manner, and that is Bosnia-Herzegovina is independent, it should be independent, just as it is spelled out in the BH Constitution. Franjo Tudjman understands the BH Constitution, and at this meeting that I -- I am familiar with it, first of all, for instance, the relationship between Franjo Tudjman and Turkey were great. Croatia and Turkey were on great terms. Hido Biscevic, who was in the Cabinet, served as an ambassador there, and he took care of all those things in Turkey. Turkey helped Croatia a great deal. It fully understood. Demirel, the Turkish president, visited Croatia several times. He fully understood Franjo Tudjman's positions. And if I may be allowed to say, in a recent TV programme, a good journalist from Croatian TV visited him in Istanbul or in Ankara. He spoke about Franjo Tudjman in -- with great praise, although he's now retired, he's no longer active in politics, and he also speaks about the number of refugees who found shelter in Turkey. But I will find this information for you. And the International Criminal Tribunal is mentioned here, the one that I am facing now. It is clearly spelled out. The position of all the structures of the government in Croatia is quite clear, of the people, of the army, of the parliament, of the government, regarding Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was all clear, regardless of all the difficulties and the shifting policies pursued by Alija Izetbegovic, the international community, the Mujahedin, the aggression against us, the arms embargo, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have just spoken about the ICTY. I was planning this question at the end of my questioning, but we may as well deal with this now, since you have addressed the issue. Lately, I've been wondering, when our Tribunal was set up, what was being said in Zagreb during the meetings which you attended, chaired by Mr. Tudjman, and also at the level of the National Defence Council. I sense that we do not have all the transcripts. There may be transcripts that have not been adduced into evidence or that were not given to the Trial Chamber because, as you know, the parties are the ones submitting documents. You are under oath, and you're supposed to tell the truth, the whole truth. During the meetings you attended in Zagreb, the very concept of this Tribunal, which was going to charge people later on, was that discussed at the level of the government?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is actually discussed here in the transcript that you have in front of you, and you will see Franjo Tudjman's position; the Tribunal is necessary, war crimes should be investigated, this will be a good thing. Mr. Milas, a lawyer who had lived in Vienna for a long time, is skeptical towards how the -- vis-a-vis how this Tribunal would adjudicate its cases. I was, of course, au courant with all of that, I wrote about it in "Hrvatski Vojnik." We advocated this Tribunal, but I meant something else, cooperation with the Tribunal in The Hague. I thought that we would be cooperating, not that we would be surrendered pursuant to any indictment that is drafted here for any old reason. There was a French proposal on how the Tribunal should be set up, on 70 pages, and this is being discussed here, and Sweden and another country, another government, with its legal experts were supposed to go through it, and then the Americans and the British came and just dumped it and they introduced a procedure that is not appropriate. The European legal system under which the Prosecutor would be an investigator, who would be cooperating with me to determine whether I was a war criminal or not, that was supposed to be the way, and not the freedom to put whatever one saw fit in an indictment, and then an indictee must prove their innocence over a period of five years; and if you take such a long time, then probably that person is guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I'm going to take a starting point that will be easy for me, because you were not concerned there. I'm speaking about Ahmici, when Ahmici happened, with all the fallout we know about in the media. Did the government meet, did Mr. Tudjman seek meetings, and did nobody say, Well, there was Ahmici, serious events took place, no doubt that is going to give rise for demands in the international community for inquiries, and this might sort of go back to us, come up? Did nobody speak about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this was talked about interminably, unfortunately, but proper investigations were not an important thing. Everybody knew what happened from a distance of 200 kilometres, 8 kilometres, 2 kilometres, but there were no good investigations in the field. The first story was that there were no rifles among the Muslims. For two years, a trial went on at this Tribunal, Your Honours, before the Court accepted that in 1993 the Muslims were armed, that they had their units, a huge quantity. Well, read -- read it for yourselves, the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but we do object. The testimony is irrelevant and it's not responsive to the President's question, whether the Ahmici incident was discussed in Zagreb among the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you're trying to tell us that there was a lack of investigation, but I put a very specific question to you. I asked whether, in Zagreb, General Tus, you, Bobetko, Susak, Tudjman, Mr. Sanader, or Mesic, whether you discussed the creation of this Tribunal, which we inevitably saw, give rise to investigations in the years to come, with possible prosecution. That was my question. Now, with regards to what you've just said, of course, the Appeals Chamber more or less confirmed what you said, but that was not the purpose of my question. I want to know whether you spoke or discussed the risk that there may be people held to account later on. I'm thinking of political and military leaders.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, not that we discussed; here there is a demand. We demanded that this Tribunal be set up. It's not only that there was talk. In this transcript, you can see that the demand is made for this Tribunal to be set up to investigate all the crimes. You saw that in "Hrvatski Vojnik," a number of texts, articles. Croatia was among the first countries to put forward that this Tribunal should be set up to investigate each and every crime, and for each criminal to be punished. This was the case continuously. You can read this transcript, what Franjo Tudjman says. I have them noted down here, but I didn't jot down the page. It's 0186750 -- the last number is 506, so it's 01867506, and I'll read it. You can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, tell us what Tudjman said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page is 40, the page 40 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, we have it here. Well, yeah, here it is. Because they would be -- the International Criminal Tribunal would be in charge of them, it would have jurisdiction over them, and this is a positive phenomenon, but we will not be able to avoid investigations into war crimes in our territory. But, of course, as I have stated quite openly, I told everyone in those diplomatic talks at state level, Please, gentlemen, there was an aggression in the Croatian territory, crimes and so on. Well, I don't want to go on quoting, but he says that the decision to establish the War Crimes Tribunal must be, and I quote: "The decision to set up the War Crimes Tribunal should be used by us in order to strengthen the legal system in our country." And then he goes on to say: "We have been always saying that we are in favour of having the rule of law." So the man in the street, our public, must understand that we have an obligation before the international community, that this is in our own interest, and therefore it must be respected from that point of view too, full stop. So let's use this, and "this" here is the International Tribunal, to put a stop to those arbitrary acts and all terrorist acts. So, Your Honours, it was not that there was just talk. Croatia supports the position of the International Criminal Tribunal, justice and the rule of law. I said this in public several times. I had some reservations regarding cooperation, the organisation, and the political influence aiming at equalising the responsibility of all sides, and I have the same criticism today. I have a great deal of material here indicating that the indictments were drafted according to political dictates from various -- yes, yes, yes, the Prosecution, yes, that's exactly as I'm saying. It's also the result of poor work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's irrelevant, Mr. President, and not responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you read the page in which Mr. Tudjman said that, if I'm to understand, that the Tribunal will make it possible to solve some crimes, and that he was not opposed to the Tribunal being created. This is important. This page is now on record. P -- yes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not an obstacle. He says, We want this because we want to have rule of law. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, you're now -- yes. So, no, we want it for the sake of the rule of law and the functioning of the legal system. That's why we want this Tribunal. We put forward its establishment. We want it, and we will support it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this explanation. Let's have a look at P02122, page 8. The meeting was held on the 27th of April, 1993. This is an important date, 27th of April, 1993. Many attendees; Tus, Tudjman, Bobetko, Greguric, Manolic, Mesic, and more. On page 8, Mr. Tudjman can be seen to say that the strategic interests of the West and Croatia is to cooperate with the Muslims, but that they had to make sure that they kept the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were of interest to Croatia. So Mr. Tudjman seems to be saying two things: First thing, the need to cooperate with Muslims; second thing, that they had to be careful and attentive. What is your comment on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, and I agree with it. Cooperation, Bosnia-Herzegovina, but not in such a way that, in the end of a peace process, we end up being in absolute minority throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, because then Muslims and Croats would be expelled from areas taken by Serbs, and then we will have done nothing, or, for instance, that Muslims would move from Sandzak and Serbia to Bosnia-Herzegovina; in other words, so that we don't face an ethnic catastrophe, occupation. Let's say what would happen if France would join with India in a joint state, and then you will see how many Frenchmen would remain living in France.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to page 16, where mention is made of ethnic cleansing. Page 16 should be called up on the screen. Here it is. Fourth paragraph, Tudjman says that: "The world is not going to allow us to execute ethnic cleansing." Well, this is a rather ambiguous sentence. We do not know whether this speaks about the Serbs or the whole world, but here Tudjman speaks about ethnic cleansing. Can you see the words, Mr. Praljak, as used by Mr. Tudjman, himself, "ethnic cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At that time, ethnic cleansing committed by Serbs -- was already committed by Serbs on a great scale. They moved 30.000 to 35.000 people into Baranja and those areas. They -- he says, We can take Knin by military means, but there would be a lot of blood. He's constantly hoping that there would be a deal, that a deal would be made, a normal political, human deal, and this is what he's saying here yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Tudjman says that the world, that is, the international community, is not going to allow ethnic cleansing, even though in this instance it is by the Serbs, in saying so, could this sentence apply to Croats as well? Might he think that the international community is not going to allow Croats, either, any ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Franjo Tudjman was hoping that the world would not allow ethnic cleansing. Unfortunately, it was allowed, and to this day it was completed, in the aftermath, quite peacefully. And if you look at the new census in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which would probably be conducted in 2011, and if you then compare it with the previous one in 1991, you will see that the ethnic cleansing was, indeed, carried out in large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Sarajevo, in Republika Srpska, and so on, so on. In Vares… The only place where it was not conducted was in areas inhabited by Croats, because Croats managed to defend their areas. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to P02302, page 7. This meeting was held on the 11th of May, 1993. This is an important date because that is two days after the 9th of May, as everybody understood. Meeting starting at 8.30 p.m. until 10.30, with Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Sanader, Mr. Mesic, Mr. Manolic, Mr. Susak, General Bobetko, General Tus, and you don't seem to have attended the meeting. On page 7, Mr. Tudjman spoke and said that: "They, the Muslims, are populating areas with refugees from Central and Eastern Bosnia. This is happening in Mostar, but also in other areas that are purely Croat places in Herzegovina, so that they changed or are changing the national composition of those places." So this raises the issue of refugees, of Muslim refugees, and in -- by reason of their number they're going to change the ethnic make-up. Is that true or overstated? What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not an exaggeration. This is correct, Your Honour. In the transcripts, you can see that I said that several times in 1992. There is an ethnic occupation of the Muslims who had been expelled from the Serbs and who moved into areas where Croats used to be in a majority of sorts. So when you have people coming in, it's not Muslims or Croats coming in; you have people coming in. And we are constructing the road of salvation. We receive them in Posusje. You are receiving people in Croatia, in Mostar, in Capljina, in Posusje. But when the war is over, those people become citizens. And you effectively lost areas, territories where you used to be in the majority, because somebody expelled Muslims and they moved into those areas. And here at the end, Tudjman says that in some places where this is going on, people are cursing Boban, Susak and Tudjman because they're arming Muslims, and they then turn their weapons against us. Well, the people are not stupid. Everybody knew everything, I assure you. And the people there, they have this historical sense, they know exactly what's going on, and it was very difficult for Franjo Tudjman to pursue this policy of arming the Muslims and then other people were killed with the same weapons. Well, somebody should try and see what it looks like, what it feels like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this text, Mr. Tudjman speaks about the situation in Mostar, and it is written here, black and white, he says that there are Muslim refugees arriving in Mostar, and the refugees are going to change the ethnic make-up of Mostar, but it is true for East and West Mostar. If Mr. Tudjman is right in saying so, when the refugees arrived in East Mostar, did they go there because it was the only place where they could go, or were they encouraged to go there so that they would actually sort of create a place that would fester in East Mostar? So what I'm trying to ascertain is whether it was somehow automatic that the Muslim refugees would go there because they had no other place to go or were they encouraged to go there. So why did they go to East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, in 1992, those refugees started coming in from Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think that at that time those ideas were not bandied about. They could have gone to Croatia, and hundreds of thousands of them did go to Croatia. But as time went by, and in particular after the fall of Jajce, all my information indicated that certain circles in the Muslim leadership were distributing a certain number of their refugees into areas where Croats and Muslims were in the balance, in terms of the number of population; Bugojno, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Mostar, and so on. The surplus went to Croatia, and a number of them were kept in that area with the wholehearted support of Croats who wanted to let them have the areas that were left vacant when the Serbs left. They distributed vacant housing to them mostly in Western Mostar, Your Honours, because there was more housing available there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you. You said earlier on that they were kept. When you said that, I remembered the testimony of witnesses who came to say that Muslims in East Mostar were free to go, but that as a matter of fact, they were prevented from doing so by the BH Army. So I'm trying to understand. If East Mostar is being shelled, is -- if East Mostar is being shelled by the HVO, if you have a civilian, a non-combatant, knowing that he's being shelled, I guess he'll want to leave, to flee. And if he does so, he reduces the ethnic composition. So by shelling, if the HVO did shell, wasn't it the aim to have these people go to re-establish the balance, but when the HVO realised that they would not leave, what was the point of keeping on shelling? At the level of the military authorities, did you have this kind of discussion? Did you discuss what was to be done, unless you tell me straight away that you did not shell but that the Serbs did?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've asked many questions, Your Honour, and you made a number of statements. First of all, I said that there were time-periods. The first wave of refugees in 1992, who came to Mostar, 30.000 to 35.000, that's one thought, that's one issue. They were taken in, and I think that among the Muslims, the Muslim leadership at the time, there was no clear idea that they should remain there. But later on, in 1993 -- in late 1992, after the fall of Jajce, so we're talking about the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, there is a clear intention that the Muslim refugees, expelled by the Serbs, should remain in the territory where Croats are in the majority or where there is a 50:50 ratio, at least to a certain number. And now as regards the period after the conflicts that started on the 30th of June, 1993, the HVO never shelled civilians, and I don't know -- well, you put that forth as an argument, but I am challenging it. So you can see that the HVO, in the six months, fired about 600 shells, Serbs fired 250 shells, and those shells were aimed at military targets. You saw how many times they set up their mortars near the hospital, and, well, there was a number of cases in Sarajevo. Their intention was to get a response and to get civilian casualties that they could then parade before the international community in order to brand the other side as criminals. Over the four and five -- four or five months of their attacks, 600 shells from our side is insignificant, in military terms. And they never targeted any civilian areas. If civilians had been targeted in Mostar, and you could see here the ethnographer, there would not have been 524 dead soldiers and no civilian casualties. I'm not saying that nobody got killed, but the HVO really made sure that even the mortars that were transported around on trucks -- and let me tell you this: When the US ambassador, and this was said here, when he came to East Mostar, they would always use that opportunity and would fire on us. We would have casualties, people were killed and wounded. And then when we responded militarily, then they would show Galbraith, Well, look, they're firing on us. Of course, Galbraith didn't see where their mortars were mounted on a car somewhere close to where he was, the mortars that are being fired to kill my lads. This was a perfidious game played throughout the war, and there are piles of very specific analyses by military observers and reporters from abroad that show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You've given me an answer for the assumptions I was making. There was no statement on my part; only assumptions. We'll now have a 20-minute break. I have about 12 transcripts, presidential transcripts, to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is back in session. Let's call up -- let's call up document P02466, page 10. We have page 10 on the screen. This is a meeting held May 20th, 1993, from 6.00 p.m. to 7.30 p.m., with Mesic, Manolic, Valentic, and many others including Bobetko, Tus, Pasalic, Tudjman, and more. During this meeting, and you see this on page 10, Mr. Tudjman says that Croatia cannot afford to lose areas that were in the Banovina, even though a good number of refugees, most of them being Muslims, are there. Croatia cannot accept either that Muslims change the demographic structure of Mostar and Travnik, because if it was -- if it did, the south of Croatia and Dalmatia would be jeopardised. Mr. Tudjman is saying a number of things. There is a clear reference to Banovina, and there is also a very clear reference to the fact that there could be modifications to Mostar and Travnik, as you said. So what is your take on this, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tudjman speaks about Banovina in precisely those terms as it is supposed to be understood. The areas, well, conditionally speaking, instead of saying areas that were inhabited by Croats in the absolute or relative majority, you cannot allow that, in the actual fact, the demographic picture should be changed by war, and there was a risk that it might be changed by aggression, in particular by the aggression of the BH Army, because we had managed to defend ourselves against Serbs. And here at the beginning, he says that Stoltenberg understood that, and so did Owen, and that he talked with Izetbegovic tete-a-tete in Split, and that this conflict with Croats that he initiated was suicide policy, and so on and so forth. And he forecasts that there would be another 140.000 Croat refugees and Muslims. Well, it's a consistent policy. Ethnic structure in a state should not be changed by war. Well, and, of course, we will protect the Croats. That's what we had fought for, and we didn't endanger anyone, in legal terms or in any other way. But Banovina has nothing to do with the state of Croatia. It's Bosnia and Herzegovina and the position of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the plans that were drawn up by the international community were always in the same vein up until Dayton or Washington, when there was this pressure that resulted in the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into two states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to June now, P02719, page 40, please. This is a conversation between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic. It's quite a long conversation. And apparently it started after 12.00 p.m., so it must have been a very important conversation. I'm interested in page 40, the one we have on the screen right now. It seems that Izetbegovic is accusing Mate Boban of being in favour of the Vance-Owen Plan, while doing everything to make sure that it cannot be implemented. So here it's a criticism of Mate Boban. Mate Boban would be playing a double game, saying, on the one hand, Yes, I agree with the Vance-Owen Plan, but, on the other hand, doing everything he can to make sure that it's not going to work. At least this is what Mr. Izetbegovic is saying. So what do you have to say regarding this? Was this Mr. Boban's traditional position or is Mr. Izetbegovic accusing him of things that are not really true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Mr. Izetbegovic is saying is entirely untrue. Croats were the first to accept the Vance-Owen Plan unreservedly, and you can -- you could see Prlic's commitment and the commitment of the HZ-HB to adopt the new structure under the Vance-Owen Plan, and the destruction thereof by the Muslim leadership in Alija Izetbegovic. And then he says, Well, we attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina [as interpreted]. That's not true. You saw the plans from April by the BH Army to attack Mostar and Central Bosnia and so on. This is a lie. Now, whether this is a lie because his people were telling him different, I don't know that, but I don't really believe that he was so ill-informed about the situation down there. After all, I, myself, pleaded with him to give me the people as we had arranged to calm the situation down. He never did anything of the sort down there, and then he said, Well, he'll call in two days or three days, he'll think about it, and so it all fell through.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. A correction for the transcript. I do apologise. Page 37, line 22, the General said: "And then he says, Well, we attacked Mostar." In the transcript, it says "Bosnia-Herzegovina," and there is a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, then Mr. Izetbegovic says here that Mate Boban -- or, rather, the HVO attacked Mostar, which is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the word "Mostar" is not there on page 38, line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has been corrected. Let's move to July now, with document P03240, page 63. This is July 6. This is the 14th session of the National Defence Council, a meeting started at 10.00 p.m. and ended at 11.30 p.m. Attending, Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Greguric, Mr. Zerkovic [phoen], Vedris, and more, but it seems that you did not attend this meeting, Mr. Praljak. However, you might know this document, and we're interested in page 63. This is right after what -- just after Valentic's words. Tudjman takes the floor again and talks about Jablanica and its hydroelectric power-plant. It seems that Mr. Tudjman asked Bobetko and Susak to seize Jablanica. So please explain what this means. What does it mean to seize Jablanica? This is July 6th. What did he mean when he said, I told Janko and Susak to seize Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really comment on it, but I can say that Mr. Valentic is talking about Herceg Novi, the problem of Herceg Novi with -- well, it's to the south of Dubrovnik. It has nothing to do with this sentence by Franjo Tudjman. It was about the water supply for Herceg Novi and the electricity supply to Dubrovnik. Herceg Novi is in Montenegro, and Herceg Novi receives its water from Dubrovnik, the Dubrovnik area, and Dubrovnik receives its power from the -- a Serb power-plant in Bosnia-Herzegovina, near Trebinje, north of Dubrovnik. And then some arrangements had to be made for Herceg Novi to get water and for Dubrovnik to get power in return. Now, what the president means when he speaks about the power-plant, well, Croatian and Bosnia-Herzegovinian electricity generation systems were linked up, and Croatian power-plants supplied Bosnia and Herzegovina with electricity. And you had a witness here, Your Honours. I questioned this witness. The power from Jablanica, well, they let the water just flow by and they didn't want to put this power-plant into the system, the electricity generation system of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. At the same time, they took electricity from Croatia to keep their power distribution system. Now, I don't know what the president managed to do in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let's move to September, P04740, page 10. This is a meeting that started at 10.00 and ended at 11.45 a.m., with Mr. Mesic, Manolic, Greguric, Susak, Granic, Bobetko, Tudjman, and Boban, and others, but you're not attending. In this meeting, Tudjman says that he talked to Bobetko and with Mate Boban, and they said that they were going to head Herceg-Bosna, as far as defence was concerned. And then he says that only the volunteers that come from Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether they're part or not of the Croatian Army, will be allowed to defend these areas. I found this quite interesting. It's on page 10, as you may see on the screen. I found it very interesting because Mr. Tudjman is mentioning volunteers, and as far as he's concerned, this can only be volunteers that come from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and not just any Croats that would not originate from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Could you tell us whether what Mr. Tudjman is saying now is in line with what you said up until now, which is that the volunteers originated from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was the position that was implemented consistently. And if I may be allowed to say -- this is an important point to make. So this is 19 -- what year, 1993? Yes, 1993. Tudjman says that as regards the position towards Belgrade, well, at that time there were rumours, and he says that they must be suppressed. And he said, I said publicly, and I have repeated, and I quote: "There is no -- there has been no agreement to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina between Croatia and Serbia. There is none." Full stop. So at this session of his core leadership, he tells them the rumours must be suppressed because there has been and there is no agreement about the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's 1993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And now we're going to move to October, to Fikret Abdic. I noted that this transcript might be of interest. P05997, please, page 3 and 4. Page 3 and 4, because Mr. Abdic is talking, and it's interesting to look at what he says on page 3 and 4. It's on the screen. Thank you. Could you please scroll up so we can -- scroll Mr. Abdic's words up, please. And then it continues further on, on the other page. He is proposing for mutual recognition of Herceg-Bosna and the autonomous province of Western Bosnia, and the signature of a peace agreement. Tudjman is going to reply, saying that the province that would be led by Abdic could be part of Croatia, but with an autonomous status. Mr. Praljak, it seems that in the framework of the discussion between Mr. Abdic and Mr. Tudjman, there seems to have been a plan which would allow Croatia to recognise the autonomous province that would be under the leadership of Abdic and that there would be a peace agreement among these two entities. And then starting from there, Mr. Tudjman is saying that this province could have a place in Croatia, could be allowed in Croatia, but would have an autonomous status. It would be an autonomous province. I think that in the former Yugoslavia, there were two autonomous provinces. I mean, of course, tell me if I'm wrong, because I'm not a specialist of Croatia, I'm just a Judge trying to understand things, but I think that at the time you had Vojvodina and Kosovo, they were two autonomous provinces within the former Yugoslavia. So I'd like to know whether they're now trying to set up an autonomous province that would be similar to that, and Croatia being allowed, through some kind of partnership agreement, to cooperate with this autonomous province as closely as possible, for example. You have the conversation on the screen between these two people. At the time, have you heard anything about this? Because if this project was true, I mean, this would mean dismantling Bosnia and Herzegovina, because one part of it could fall under the realm of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, at that time there were no autonomous provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina. They had already been abolished, and very much so, with the destruction of the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and this unilateral destruction was something that nobody in the world responded to. The Serbian leadership, headed by Slobodan Milosevic, simply abolished two autonomous provinces without any legal foundation. Vojvodina and Kosovo. That’s number one. Number two, here Mr. Abdic is not talking about the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the recognition of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, of sorts, and then his autonomous province, and he took part in the talks in Geneva, so he did have an autonomous province of sorts. Now, as to its significance, nobody knew what would get recognised in the end, because as you could see, it changed all the time. And he says here, Croatia is our support. We rely on it. We will use the Croatian state infrastructure. Well, this is far removed from any secession. We're talking about strategic interests here, and Mr. Abdic says Bosnia, as a whole, is gravitating towards Croatia, of course those parts that were not controlled by the Serbs, and this is entirely true. So this is a conversation between two people, what would happen if things turned out in this way or that, because at that time nobody knew what the fate of Bosnia would be. At that time, Your Honours, there was a great deal of talk already in all diplomatic contexts and so on that after the war, Bosnia-Herzegovina would find it difficult to survive and that perhaps it was better, so this is just taking some options into consideration. But there were no agreements, or treaties, or anything, or signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you are right, Mr. Abdic is talking about recognition by the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and vice versa. Why is it that this never came to? Politically, it would have been a good way to dismantle part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to have an agreement with a good number of Muslims in the framework of mutual recognition. So Tudjman and Abdic are mentioning this plan, but why is it that it never came to anything? What prevented it from being implemented?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it never occurred to anyone to implement it without the confirmation or the green light of the international community. These were just talks about what would happen if this were to be received, if the green light were to be received from the Muslims, from the Croats, from the Serbs; Muslims and Alija Izetbegovic, of course, indicating that a large portion of the Muslim leadership wanted an independent state, and I provided evidence to that effect. The only problem was the -- how much territory would be allotted to each side. So it was a war about territory, it was not a war about people wanting to live in a certain way, on their own. Not on the Croatian side. But -- so this did not come to pass for a very simple reason; because the Americans would at one point get involved more heavily and would start exerting pressure on Tudjman and Izetbegovic to create a federation and a confederation with Croatia, so a federation of Croats and Muslims in the areas that had not been taken by the Serbs, followed by a confederal treaty that would tie this federation with the Republic of Croatia, which was clearly spelled out in the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, General Praljak, did Fikret Abdic participate in the Geneva negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some negotiations, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you know, did he have an international stature or was he just not very important?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the combinations. They didn't consider him to be especially important, but when there was an emphasis on the division, then they accepted him. But when this was pushed in the background, they didn't -- no longer accepted him. That depended on the political games.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's leave Mr. Abdic, and we will now move to November, just a few days before you actually depart, leave. Page P06454 -- document P06454. It's a meeting held in Zagreb on November 5th in Villa Dalmatia -- no, it's not in Zagreb, this is a meeting that was held in Split. The attendants are Mr. Tudjman, apparently with Boban, Prlic, and yourself, as well as Petkovic. Do you remember being in that villa November 5th?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this the presidential residence? What exactly is this villa?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It used to belong to Tito. It was one of the villas that existed in every larger town all over Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 1, Tudjman says that the problem of republic Herzegovina is of interest to the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also the Croatian people in the future of the Croatian state and its borders. It's quite an interesting sentence. Mr. Tudjman is clearly stating that this -- the problem of Bosnia-Herzegovina is the problem of the Croatian people and Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also a problem for the Croatian state, and that this might have some consequences on the borders. What did he mean? Did he want to just highlight that the problem was extremely complex?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He explicitly, in dozens of places, says that the problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a political, historical, psychological problem, it's a highly complex problem in those terms, and that the international community often fails to under the complexity of the problem, and that's what he's repeating here. The problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the problem of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. But if you look at the map, Your Honours, the map that you have seen hundreds of times, of course it is important whether in Bihac, for instance, which is in the hinterland of Knin and Croatia, whether there would be Muslims or Serbs there, just as it is very important who would be on the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina; Croats in Herceg-Bosna or some other side, which would be inimical. In light of the fact that it took such a long time to establish peace, Franjo Tudjman did not have any guarantees. For instance, if Muslims and Serbs reached an agreement and if they had taken the south of Croatia, nobody in the world would have batted an eyelid, just as nobody has batted an eyelid for Cyprus or any other problem. We should not be overly optimistic about the world politics. So his position is crystal clear here. Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina must decide their own fate, but Croatia, because they're Croats and because Croatia shares the border with this country, has a vital interest in how this will be solved. And this was my position at the time, and it is my position now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to page 2. Indeed, we're going to have Provinces 3 and 8 addressed by Mr. Tudjman. I hadn't planned this question originally, but I think it's important to put it to you. Page 2, here it is. Last paragraph, last line. In a very clear fashion, Mr. Tudjman speaks about the Vance-Owen Plan, and he says that there should be a union of the republics, of the Croatian and Muslim republics, which explains all the documents we have seen, because early, at the beginning of the trial, I was very surprised when I saw the words "union of republics," and I must confess that I didn't know what it meant at all, but as time went by, I understood what it was about. And here, Mr. Tudjman says that the actual solution is a confederation, a final confederation, so there will be a union of republics to be followed by a confederation with Croatia. What was your take on this? Mr. Tudjman, I was going to say. Yes, Mr. Praljak, but you, too, attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I'm not Tudjman. He was highly educated, smart, wise. I'm less so, although I don't underestimate myself. So, very clearly, the Muslim offensive fell through, and given what had been happening in the months that preceded this time, the president of a state says calmly, Look, we'll put together a union of Muslims and Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then he says, And have as close ties as possible with Croatia, including a confederation. He is proposing this, he's not imposing it. And he says, And that there should be as close ties as possible, with Croatia, of course, all the way up to a possible confederation with Croatia. And the Americans picked up on that later on as the basis for the Washington Agreement. But once they no longer needed it, they just set it aside. They signed it, and then at one point it was as if it never existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether your memory is correct, but since Mr. Prlic is not present, I'm not going to insist. If he had been here, I would have called up that page in particular. But this was page 53. I don't have it with me, but on page 53, Mr. Prlic said that within Herceg-Bosna, the quality of the staff was not sufficient. And you, yourself, said that the level of military competence was very low within the HVO. Do you remember that? You said that here orally, but there is evidence. That's the document in which Prlic talks about the poor quality of the men, and you tie in and say that, yes, changes would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I partly recall Mr. Prlic's intervention, and I read it subsequently. I fully agree with his discussion, and I, of course, remember well my own contribution. If I can put it briefly in two minutes, Your Honour, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially from Herzegovina, but also very much so from Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were many people who emigrated right after 1945. That's the first thing. The second thing: An enormous mass of people from the poor areas left to work abroad. In terms of percentage, many more Croats left than the members of other ethnicities. That's why the census in 1991 does not reflect accurately the totality of Croats, because a great many Croats from Germany, Switzerland and Austria did not participate in this census.
