Thirdly, for example, in Western Herzegovina, there was the fact of not a single factory. Because of that, all of us who left Western Herzegovina stayed mostly in Croatia. Only later, some people remained in Zagreb. A great many Herzegovinians and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were against the order of things, against the system in the former Yugoslavia. Many of them were imprisoned. In comparison with the two other peoples, among the Croatian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were very few intellectuals left. Many, many people from Herzegovina left and stayed in Zagreb, thousands upon thousands, after receiving their degrees. Therefore, not enough qualified personnel remained; that is to say, people who, under such circumstances, could be made useful. They simply did not return from Zagreb. The odd few, including myself, did. That included the army, the civilian life. And in such conditions, we were short of people who could do quality work. This is what it's all about, and that's what the truth of the matter was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're still in November, but now the next day, because on the next day there was a meeting. P06485, page 2, please. This was in the Presidential Palace, on the 6th of November, with Mr. Tudjman. I'm interested in what he said on page 2. I'll first check that you have that page before you. He said it was important to take control of Gornji Vakuf, but to stay covered by sending volunteers only. And he added that he might even send directly an HBV [as interpreted] brigade to Mostar so that an HVO brigade would be available, it being specified that the brigade would only carry out defensive actions. So Mr. Tudjman mentioned two things here. He speaks about Gornji Vakuf, but he says there should be volunteers there, and he also envisions that there could be a brigade of the Croatian Army in Mostar so that an HVO brigade could be made available. But if there is an HV brigade, it would only be engaged for defensive action. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what the president mentioned. The issue of Gornji Vakuf being taken over, and you can see that the same opinion was shared by many military analysts and foreigners who discussed this, was the issue of our survival. If lines were broken through at Gornji Vakuf and Rama, save for a small part of Western Herzegovina, there would be no other location for us to establish secondary lines. Second of all, unfortunately, the Muslim desire for conquest in the direction of the sea, i.e., south of Mostar, did not cease at that moment, and Mr. Franjo Tudjman said that should that happen and they advanced further towards Mostar, the use of Croatian Army would not be excluded. Concerning Mr. Izetbegovic and his discussion on the number of Muslims in Central Bosnia, I prepared an excerpt from the 1991 -- sorry, 1981 to 1991 census for Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Kresevo, and Vares. Here it is. It is signed. If you wish, you may take it as evidence that Mr. Izetbegovic was not telling the truth. He talked about the facts as they stood in the ethnically-occupied part of Western Bosnia, Central Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me, but a correction for the transcript. Page 50, lines 1, 2 and 3, it is misstated that the general said that "it was our decision to liberate the part held by the Muslims." The General actually said it was a wish on the part of the Muslims to occupy territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their desire to occupy did not cease, and in the transcript it turned out that it was the Croats who were trying to do that. You must slow down, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Although a truce was signed, an offensive on the part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was well underway, including the areas south of Mostar. That is why Tudjman envisaged a possibility that the HV would assist the HVO so as to prevent any further occupation of Croatian areas. That did not happen, but I believe his decision was logical because the Muslims had, by that time, signed the truce which they did not abide by, and the war continued into 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, keep this document, please. When it comes to your defence or to your strategy of defence in my questions, you can address this document. I first want to finish with the transcripts. Only very few are left. Can we call up P07198.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I apologise for the interruption. I know that various counsel have often very helpfully risen when they feel that corrections need to be made to the transcript. I'm not sure that what just happened here was sort of a misinterpretation on the part of the interpreters in the booth that counsel drew our attention to or whether, in fact, it was more in the nature of a suggested clarification. And I don't know and I'm not making any allegations, but I think that it wasn't a very -- it wasn't the very normal sort of correction where we have a year or a word that's clarified or corrected. And so I think that on this point, I think that when we go back to finalise the transcript, it would be useful to listen to what the general said, see whether, in fact, it was correctly interpreted and appearing in the transcript, and if so, then obviously any clarification that he's made can remain on the transcript. But I think that just to sort of go back and make corrections without actually double-checking whether they're necessary is something that should be done in this one instance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, yes, you have a response?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not a suggestion to the general. We truly wanted to correct the transcript. You know that after each hearing, we submit verification requests should we come across problematic areas, and we have just filed that the general's contribution be listened to and clarifications be made, and then we will make sure what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're free to listen to what I said. I did say what the clarification was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to P07198, page 21, pages 21 and 22. This meeting was held after you left, since it was on the 13th of December, 1993. There are many attendees, but at some point you were mentioned. I don't know where you were on that date, but obviously you did not attend that meeting. But General Tudjman spoke about you. That's towards the end of the last-but-one paragraph. We see your name, "General Praljak." During the meeting, Tudjman said that he had taken steps, sent men to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that General Praljak thought that the Croats were doing something wrong in Bosnia and Herzegovina; that he had told Praljak to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that 14 days later, General Praljak admitted that he was wrong. What do you have to say to what Tudjman said about you at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is rather brief and a bit unclear, Your Honour. Oftentimes, I had certain objections to the type of behaviour of certain Croatian officials. Sometimes there seemed to be too much anger or emotional involvement when we heard about things that the Muslims had done. But throughout that period, until May, I was still trying to persuade them that we should be working on, as we were, that common language should be found with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In May, I came back and I told Franjo Tudjman that it is my forecast that the determinants of political thought would win over an attempt to establish a sound union with the Muslims. I told him, It's finished now, they are attacking us. And that was the reason why I asked to be sent down there to help. This has to do with certain, say, mistakes; for example, the problem of registering vehicles. Muslims were objecting to the HZ-HB sign on the plate, but, on the other hand, Austrians would not honour any green card, in terms of insurance for cars from Sarajevo. There were hundreds of details of technical nature, but are often misinterpreted. To the Muslims, this meant, yes, they're trying to impose their registration plates, but without such plates one could not go to Austria or Switzerland, because you wouldn't get the right papers. But then I put it crystal clear that the Muslim decision to attack the HVO towards the end of May and in June had ripened by that time and that they will use all of their military assets to attack. That's why I said I was wrong even in the attempts to persuade those people. This is what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take page 22, because there's a detail that drew my attention. I would like you to speak to it. Same document, page 22. Go to the second paragraph, where he mentions mistakes. Tudjman is going to speak about Ahmici and about Stupni Do, and he said this is terrible. But I'm interested in what follows, because we see plural pronoun "they," and I'm wondering who they are, "they." They must be the Muslims. And Tudjman said: "Together with the English, and they donned black uniforms, and all this was filmed. All this was to compromise Croatia." So what did Mr. Tudjman want to say about Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have been so fast that much of what you have said is completely lost. So you have to go back to where you started answering the President. There's nothing in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please start again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Franjo Tudjman's basic assertion about Ahmici and Stupni Do was that it was horrific, it was horror. The second thing is what we knew and what I'm repeating here at this Tribunal, starting with the KOS and various Muslim units which were active under Alija Izetbegovic's guide-lines, such as Sevas [phoen], Black Swans, as well as in terms of different international players who had unclearly defined wishes. All of those aided and assisted the crimes in their commission, in terms of what security services would do in such situations. What horrified us was that there were thousand-fold more information about Ahmici than you would have Uzdol, Doljani, and so on and so forth, about Konjic. This could not have been accidental. This is no mere chance. On Croatian Television, according to some of my research, Ahmici were mentioned at least a thousand times in different context. As for the Trusina crime near Konjic, only twice, only 2 percentiles. This was an organised production of chaos, of lies and deceit, in which hundreds of secret services, dozens of services, assisted in the commission or carrying out of such dirty work, blaming Croatia. Franjo Tudjman was desperate by that point in time because he did not know who it was that was doing that and why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, who was in charge of and controlling Croatian TV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian government, seemingly, but you had former employees in the television company, in the broadcasting company. No purge was carried out in Croatia, no idealogical purge, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But wouldn't it then have been for the Croatian government to see that the information is less one-sided, less than you now say it was? Who else could have changed that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian government could, if it had been able to, but they were not, because if you touched a single journalist in Croatia, all institutions, starting with Amnesty International downwards, would keep repeating that Croatia was suppressing freedom of journalistic reporting. These people were formerly employed in the dictatorship -- dictatorial system for decades. Many of them were in favour of Yugoslavia rather than Croatia. But you could not touch them; otherwise, that would constitute an attack on the freedom of expression of a single journalist. And when you put it all together, you realise that you have Ahmici mentioned 1.000 times, and Trusina only twice, then you realise there was something there. And I won't even mention other instances. I only had the right once, one single time to say publicly on television, that I wasn't correct or -- but any journalist could say thousands -- dozens upon dozens of times that it was Praljak who brought the Old Bridge in Mostar down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I leave it at that. I'm not entirely convinced. There are also other media and so forth. But leaving that aside, I would like to point to something that I read on page 22 in this transcript, and that's where the President Tudjman says: "So let's --" I quote: "So let's try and influence the Muslim leadership to stop the war with the Croats and agree on the demarcation that would be acceptable to Croatia ." Why does he say that a demarcation within Bosnia and Herzegovina, as I understand it, should be acceptable to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To protect the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Judge Trechsel, demarcation in Bosnia-Herzegovina of such nature so as to make it acceptable. After all, Croatia had to take care of the people down there in an exceptional manner. It could not consent to all Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina being driven out. This was a sense of duty, to assist the people there, and this was our policy throughout. But this is drawing boundaries in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In such discussions you cannot always put it strictly in the context of demarcation between Croats and Muslims. These are shortened speeches which were typed out. But the gist, the meaning of the sentence is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, too, the meaning is clear. He speaks of an agreement, which can only be an agreement between the Croats of Herceg-Bosna and the Muslims of Herceg-Bosna. Now, why -- why should Croatia have to be content? As a guardian over the Croats of Herceg-Bosna, does Tudjman think that they are not able -- when they pass an agreement, that they cannot be trusted? I do not understand why the Republic of Croatia must be contented.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, because if the Muslims ... it was the time of their offensive. Croatia could not be content, if the HVO loses the war down there and then has to sign an agreement with the Muslims, that it only had the right to Western Herzegovina. Of course the Croatia had an interest there. It had an interest in Bosnia-Herzegovina to protect the Croatian population in a way that nothing would be taken away from anyone, but that we should not be defeated either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is not what it says here. He says, Let us agree on a demarcation. Influence the Muslim leadership. Stop the war with the Croats. Agree on a demarcation, which, of course, must be acceptable to the Croats and to the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But why must that be acceptable to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, have a look, please. He says this: "Let us try," and I quote, "to influence the Muslim leadership." "Let us try to influence the Muslim leadership," so that they would cease waging war against Croats, so that they would consent to that demarcation, or such a demarcation that would be acceptable for Croatia, so that in such a way preconditions could be made in which Croats in Sarajevo could remain - there were 30.000 of them - and so that we remain in Central Bosnia, that the Croats in Central Bosnia remain there, full stop. And then later, you understand, they will have to seek support in the West. In other words, it is important now to explain to the Muslims that they should cease their attacks, that a demarcation line is drawn in such a way that Croats remain in Central Bosnia and Sarajevo, and then, as he thought, support should be sought from the West. Franjo Tudjman held it in a higher regard than I do, it seems. This would be acceptable for Croatia in that way, because Franjo Tudjman was, under constitution, tasked with securing such interests, much as France had its interests in all citizens of France as well as those in Quebec, and Italy takes care of its citizens outside Italy as well. Any country would do that. Much the same way, we were trying to take care of that issue. That is why, after all of what was said about Bosnia-Herzegovina, one issue remained was whether Croatia would be satisfied with it. Of course, it should be happy in preserving Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the territories where they live and in which, in the past, they had been in absolute majority, at least in terms of -- or even in terms of religion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, let's now move to P07464, page 54. This is a meeting held on January 2nd, 1994. You are not attending. It's at 10.45 a.m. with Susak, Sagmatic [phoen], Sarinic, Tudjman, and others. On page 54, it's quite interesting, notably regarding what Mr. Tudjman says. His words are in the middle of this page. I'll sum it up. He says that if the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina would go to Serbia, would join Serbia, Herceg-Bosna would join Croatia. And he adds that if the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina join Serbia, the Croats can absolutely not accept to stay in the union alone. So Mr. Tudjman is actually talking about the entire problem of Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, and the idea he's putting forth is the following. He says that if the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., of Republika Srpska, join Serbia, then the Croats of Herceg-Bosna must join Croatia. This is what he is stating in this paragraph. Was this how the debate was coined in January 1994? No one knew what the outcome was going to be. Everyone knew about the existence of Republika Srpska. So what can you tell us about all this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your interpretation is quite correct, and what is written here is also quite correct. You saw, in the previous excerpt, that Tudjman is speaking about the survival. The key word here is not the satisfaction of Croatia, but the survival of Croats in Sarajevo and the survival of Croats in Central Bosnia. And it is logical -- well, he says here if the international community, and this had already been mooted, if it allows Republika Srpska to leave the union, and Alija had already signed such an agreement in September 1993 with them, then the Republic of Herceg-Bosna had the same right to leave that union because it would simply disappear. It would be overwhelmed by the majority of the other people. It is a demographic issue, not a legal issue. There are no Croats left in Vares, in Sarajevo, and in other places. Look at the situation as it is now. The demographic trends after the war are quite clear. And, secondly, he says here, But then the Muslim union, or, rather, the Muslim republic, what we are offering to them is all ties with Croatia, and he goes on to enumerate. With the Bosnian republic, the Croatia state is ready to enter into all kinds of treaties, all the way up to a confederal treaty or any other kind of union they wish to have. Well, there you have it. Again there is an offer of a union that is made to the Muslims in any shape and form they want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We still have three transcripts to go through. P07475, page 6, first. This is a meeting with Tudjman, Susak, Bobetko, held at the Presidential Palace. I believe this transcript was very important for the following reason. I assume that you have read all the judgements that were rendered by this Tribunal; the Naletilic case, the Kordic case, and the Blaskic case. I'm sure you know that in his submissions, the Prosecutor is taking up all that; notably, the problem of total control. You know that the Appeals Chamber defines overall control characterizing an international conflict by the fact that Croatia was allowed to participate in the military operations. Overall control goes beyond effective control. You have to have the involvement in military operations. At least that is the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber. Now, of course, I don't follow everything that the Appeals Chamber says, but I do look at everything and others' submissions, so I looked at the transcript. And obviously here on the screen we see that the people who attended this meeting are looking very closely at the military operations occurring in Busovaca and other places. I'm not going through the entire page -- all the pages, but you see that all the attendants here are really looking very closely into what is happening militarily wise. So could you tell us why Mr. Tudjman, who is the leader of Croatia, is organising this meeting, this hour-long meeting? It's longer than that, actually, an hour and a half. And in this -- during this meeting, they really look very closely and they scrutinize the military operations. But these are events that are occurring in another state, not in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to grasp this, for a very simple reason. Military operations are considered at the Joint Chiefs of Staff in the US Army for every single point on the globe, and the French troops are in Africa, in the Horn of Africa and so on. There were no actions, but the whole thing begins with the defence minister's statement in "Oslobodjenje" that the BH Army needs to capture everything all the way down to the coast, and that's what they had been doing for months. Well, for five months, they had been attacking the area. And it is the duty of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While you are talking, I would like the Registrar to call up page 7 of this. But you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it is understandable, if you look at what I said before, it is necessary to make sure that the Croatian people in Central Bosnia survive; the survival of the Croats in Sarajevo, the survival. For God's sake, we have to make sure that the people survive. If the French and the Americans and all those who could didn't do anything to ensure it, for the people in Srebrenica and Bihac to survive, Franjo Tudjman is sticking to the elementary human way of thinking. He didn't sign the treaty on a safe area and then let whoever wanted to do what they wanted. He cares about the survival of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Bosnia-Herzegovina. He didn't want to see another 300.000 people expelled, for us to be discussing here whether this is international conflict or not. Down there, you would have had genocide, expulsion and ethnic cleansing, and we would have two more people sitting in the dock here. And that would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please look at the middle of the page. Dreznica, is that in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's, yeah, further up from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, just check what Mr. Tudjman is saying, verbatim. He says, and I quote: "Wait a minute." He's talking to Bobetko: "Wait a minute, Janko." Janko is Bobetko; right? "If you take," and he then says: "If we take Dreznica," He says "we." "We." "We," that's the Croats from Zagreb. Just look at what he's saying. When you read this sentence, General Praljak, I must say that you really -- one really feels that Tudjman, Bobetko and Susak are supervising the military operations going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they are looking very closely at what's happening on the field. And let me add one thing. They seem to be doing this by looking at a map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's done on the basis of the map of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which was -- which was included in the list. And what he says here, "we," well, he's talking about Croats, and you are not talking in legal terms when you're sitting at the table; you're talking in non-legal terms here. But here he says, Janko, taking Dreznica, which of course, well, President Tudjman doesn't know that, he says, but, We would then show that this was a major offensive. First of all, it would not be. And, secondly, he says, Well, never mind Dreznica. It is important to ensure the survival of Croats in Central Bosnia. And Muslimovic, or whatever his name is, General whoever, Alagic, is taken -- they had already taken Vares. They had taken Fojnica. They had taken Travnik. They moved their own people there. And this is an effort to ensure the survival of the remnants of Croats, so few were left there. And this is all about the road from Gornji Vakuf to Kiseljak, to dig it through so that we can establish communications with them. No offensive, no taking of territory, but salvation. And it all started with the Muslims saying, We want to reach the western borders. You cannot divide the two. You cannot talk about what Franjo Tudjman is doing unless you know what the enemy is doing at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is kindly asked to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is: Where do you defend the French borders? America is defending its borders, strategically speaking, wherever it is under attack - yes, I will slow down - in Afghanistan, in Iraq, and perhaps tomorrow in North Korea. And if Iran goes on with its nuclear programme, the question is: Who's going to bomb it? Well, these are threats, and you have to respond to threats with something. And here we're not talking about taking territory, not waging war. And this all fell through, Your Honours. Nothing came of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: You're already going very much beyond the questions and the realities of the life, so speaking about US actions, North Korea, et cetera, it is really better if you would refrain from it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe my colleague has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I would invite you to look at the next page, page 8. I read the following. It's practically the second sentence : "Whence this border, if we manage to hold it militarily and politically, too, therefore to hold Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, and to get Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and this, we must get in order to have 17.5 per cent." This is not -- if one reads Mr. Tudjman, this is not about saving the people and survival. It is about having 17.5 per cent. What is your commentary on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's really difficult for me to talk about it here at this trial. Well, Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, who killed all those Croats in Bugojno in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not asking about who killed someone or not. And you have said it's difficult for you to talk about it. You don't have to. If you say, "I don't really know, I don't have a clear answer on this," nobody's going to blame you for it. I mean, you were not there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was there, first of all, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. I was there; not at the meeting. I was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I was only talking about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to be at the meeting to know that 17.5 per cent is less territory than there is population in the Republic of Croatia and that, in terms of land registry books, Croats have 36 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina as their property. And why would it mean to capture territory if you are defending 17.5 per cent of the territory that we inhabited? And how could it refer to the capturing of Bugojno, where we had been expelled, killed? The sense can be found in the connections, and the sense of the language lies in the context. Judge Prandler, I am not getting out of our boundaries. The context gives meaning to words, and taking them out of the context serves no purpose. I'm sorry. Franjo Tudjman, the territory is 2 per cent less than the number of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is not a question of capturing. This is a question of salvaging, against -- in the face of a ruthless attack first by the Serbs and then by the BH Army. So what are we talking about here? We were supposed to let them kill us, expel us, slaughter us, take everybody in, arm the BH Army, and then that would be the only circumstance in which we would not be guilty. And I do not accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I did not speak about what anybody was supposed to do, or not to do, or tolerated. I just asked for an explanation of this sentence regarding 17.5 per cent. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the transcript before last, P07485, if we could please have page 7 on the screen. This is the 34th session of the National Defence Council, with Greguric, Tudjman, Bobetko, Susak, and so forth and so on. You did not attend this meeting, but we know that at first you were in the National Defence Council. Does this mean that when you came back, you were banned from taking part in these kinds of meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not prohibit me, but at one point I volunteered to leave the council. And if you want to know the reason, I'll share it with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that you left this council on your own volition. Very well. Let me address what Tudjman is saying about Mate Boban. It's on page 7, and I believe it's quite interesting. According to what he says, he says he's been informed of Mate Boban's retirement; that he has informed people about it, complaining that Boban was the main obstacle to cooperation with Muslims. And he says that he was not the one who appointed him in the first place. That's what he says. So what's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not about what I think. I know what happened. I made this demand in Split. I made myself very clear. I asked for possible removal from office of Mr. Boban, but not for those reasons, but because Herceg-Bosna had to be better organised. This pressure on Franjo Tudjman to remove Mate Boban from office came as pressure on the weaker side. Everybody pisses on a rabbit. That's a fact of international relations. Whoever is the weaker side gets to feel the pressure. And that's why I left the National Defence and Security Council, because I no longer wanted to condone this appeasement policy because we were weaker. Our policy was consistent and just, and the fact that somebody wanted to stop the war double quick by forcing the weaker side to accept any kind of compromise, I was no longer willing to accept it. And that is how the signature in Dayton -- the signature of the Dayton Accords ended up. Serbs got their own state, and Croats lost everything, their identity, because the weaker side gets pissed on. I didn't want to accept it then, I do not accept it now. Mate Boban was not opposed to the cooperation with Muslims. He was against this policy of appeasing Muslims and Serbs at the expense of their own -- of his own people, beyond every acceptable measure, and in this sense he was right. And I, personally, was against his involvement in the effort to structure HZ-HB better, and I explained how, in order to be able to withstand every pressure, whether it’s coming from the US, France or anywhere else, a pressure which was unjust, unprincipled, illogical and which created a state which has not survived today. After 15 years, the situation is much worse now than it was during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I didn't want to interrupt you, but I believe that there is an important departure in the text of the transcript. When you spoke, I believe that you wanted to say the opposite, and I quote here from line 4: "And I personally was against his involvement in the effort to structure HZ-HB better in order to be able to withstand every pressure from the US, from France, wherever." I believe that, the contrary, you were complaining a few minutes ago about Boban, that he was not strong enough to stand up and to do something, kind of reorganisation as far as the structure of the unity and the state was concerned, and that is why now you said something else. Would you clarify this, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Precisely so. In a way, in Split, and I don't think that everything is in the transcript, when I criticised Mate Boban, that was precisely along the lines that you've just presented to us. It was because -- and it might be because of the fact that he went to those meetings, and some omissions in terms of information and for failing to reduce the amount of bad democracy in the municipalities, failing to impose a more strong -- a stronger structure of administration in Herceg-Bosna, and this is where his responsibility lies, to my mind. His guilt has been fabricated here, in terms of his refusal to cooperate with the Muslims, because Franjo Tudjman was being forced, and he had been blackmailed in terms of Croatian territories taken by Serbs, he was constantly being blackmailed, that Croatia forced Mate Boban to give in, at the expense of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this is what happened in Dayton. Croats had to give in, and their fate in Bosnia and Herzegovina is very bad. And Serbs got, as their reward, a state after everything that happened down there. This is how world politics is run. It's powerful, but I beg to differ with it, and this is why I complained and why I demanded that I be allowed to withdraw from the National Security and Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, perhaps you have noted, on page 7, at end of the middle paragraph, the President Tudjman speaks of a conference and agreement with International Administration of the European Union, "over Mostar that is usually recognised as the capital of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Can you explain this somewhat surprising statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they wanted some kind of special administration over Mostar. And why just over Mostar, we don't know that. And they passed an electoral law in Mostar that is still in force which is unique in the whole world. Regardless of how many inhabitants there are, there must be parity between Croats and Muslims. This parity need not be achieved in Tuzla, in Sarajevo, but it has to be achieved in Mostar. And this is what I'm talking about. The weaker side is being killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You may have missed my point. It's the first time that I hear that Mostar is being regarded as the capital, not of Herceg-Bosna, of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, these are just mistakes in those shorthand transcripts. The capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina, well, that's Sarajevo. It's just a mistake that one has to have in those kinds of transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I have overlapped. I was saying that I had supposed so, but wanted to have it clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. The basic translation error of the presidential transcripts lies in the fact that in the English text, it says: "Mostar is usually recognised." In the Croatian, it says: "Mostar that is usually recognised as the capital." The basic meaning in Croatian would be -- [In English] "Is recognised as capital city." [Interpretation] So usually in the English is or should be "by the way recognised." This was aside on the part of the presidents. That's not the gist of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last transcript and then we'll have the break. P07910. P07910, page 35, please. The first two paragraphs, once again this is about a meeting that was held on the 20th of February, 1994, from 9.00 to 11.00 in the morning, with Susak, Zubak, Granic, Sokol, Matic, Akmadzic, and Kaspar, and Mr. Tudjman. Tudjman said that the Croats should make sure that the Muslims do not influence the Croats in Herceg-Bosna, that they should accept -- because now they're forced to by the world, they should accept the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whilst making sure that the Croatian region in Bosnia and Croatia are not Islamicized. So Mr. Tudjman is now saying that there is a non-Islamicization. He deems that as a positive thing, but he adds that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina should not let themselves be influenced by the Muslims. What is your take on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Islamicization, Your Honour, to a great degree. This is fear. We're talking about fear here, the fear of Muslims, by increasing their numbers by at least 50 per cent, would simply take over dominance over Croats, and the principle of one man, one vote. And Susak was trying to persuade Tudjman to enter a confederative relationship with the Muslims, who numbered 2.400.000. Otherwise -- and that they feared to accept that, fearing the influence of the Arabic countries. And that is what we feared. This concerned over 50 per cent of all Croats. This was not a mere 50 per cent of the population. I could discuss this for hours, in terms of France, Algeria, and you know that better than I do. This is fear. This has to do with reconciling the wishes of the West, that is strong, with the national interests of Croatia, although the Croatian national interests were not against anyone and we had all the right to bear our national interests in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's time for a break, a 20-minute break. And after the break, we'll have a document from list 6, 4D01317, but it's got another number, P00592.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in session. So we have document -- or the document here. Let's go to Article 27. This is Article 27. General Praljak, I thought it was necessary to present to you this Article 27, compared to your responsibility as set forth in our Article 7(3). I've had questions for you already, but we have to be comprehensive with regard to the scope of responsibility of a military commander who, in this case, was at the highest level, since you were the HVO military commander. This is a Decree on Military Courts. I shall not go into the detail of each and every article, but I thought this Article 27 is important, because it seems - I insist on the word "seems" - it seems to impose on a military commander, no matter what his rank is, the obligation to take all necessary steps and measures to prevent crimes, to also launch inquiries and order investigations. Now, let's look at paragraph 2 in Article 27. The military prosecutor has to be informed. When we were at another document, you said that you just informed the SIS and the military police. I see a contradiction between this article, that imposes on you the obligation to be informed of everything, and the fact that you inform a service that is free not to do anything at all. So first question: When you took up your position, did you know of the existence of Article 27?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I knew it from before, from the Croatian Army, because there is a similar article to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your recollection, who was the military prosecutor for Mostar and the Mostar area? Second question: Did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was in charge for the Mostar area. A lot of time has passed, and because of everything that took place, I don't seem to be able to recall his name. I never met him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had no meeting with him. Let's take a hypothetical case. It will make it easier to understand. Let us imagine that you have, among your men, a soldier who committed a crime, raped a civilian person, and you prosecute that man. Did it happen to you that you ordered prosecutions, and did you seek to remain in touch with the follow-up proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain cases, yes; in others, no, depending on whether I knew and who took over the duty to do so. First of all, the emphasis here is put on prevention. Crimes can be best prevented by what we had been doing, and that is to say, by educating. Second of all, we have a mention of the company commander being the least senior officer in charge of a territory. If that company commander knew or witnessed the commission of a crime, he was obligated to undertake these measures. Unfortunately, crimes were committed covertly, at night, and out of control. That is why frequently it would be learned that something had been done. However, the investigation was made all that more difficult for the commander, if he did not see that or if no one reported it to him. After that, what happened is what would happen in any other, say, civilian society; an inquiry -- an investigation is launched. I can cite a number of examples. If I were present, I would bring such a person to justice, and any of my junior officers were obliged to do so, down to the level of company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question on this topic before moving on. Remember, we saw a report on crimes in Prozor/Rama, in which it was said that a military policeman did commit wrongdoings. If the commander gives an assignment to the military police, and the military police themselves are guilty of crimes, nothing will happen. So in such a situation where you had doubt and suspicions regarding the military police, what did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report you saw and the reports that came in came either from the SIS or from the military police themselves and were addressed to those people tasked with undertaking measures. Hence -- and of course, Your Honours, such investigations were carried out, and I can enumerate many, although Mr. Coric would be better at that, in terms of statistics and numbers. But, say, in Rama, at night you can hear shooting, disorder. But who was it that was doing it? So the question was not whether it was being done, but who did that. Unfortunately, you cannot see people doing that. They did such things secretly. And when you are powerless to detect the perpetrators, you try to -- and as I told you on several occasions about the meetings, educating people, asking them to investigate and report, to do everything possible. Unfortunately, frequently not much could be done, because I believe you can imagine how things were -- looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is enough on this topic. I'll now move to the last part of my questions, in two parts. First I'll have questions without going to documents. These questions are based on your defence as spelled out in your pre-trial brief, following the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, so my questions will be general ones. And once this is done, I shall return to your submissions of the 9th of April, and I shall focus on specific paragraphs in your submissions. I'll have some 50 documents to put to you then. The essential part for you is your defence, as you set it forth in your submissions. And, firstly, you say that the Prosecution caricatures the historic reality. Could you expand on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what my attorneys wanted to say by the exercise of caricaturing a historical past. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question. Did you read your lawyers' pre-trial brief or not? I know that you did not read the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, but did you read the one written by your lawyers, because if you don't read the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, that can be understood, but, I mean, your strategy of defence, as presented by your counsel, was not read by you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I partially did leaf through, but not in detail. I partially hoped that we would put forth clear facts in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is stated that the Prosecution sort of hid the part played by the Serbs and by the JNA. Can you tell us to what extent or in which way what the Serbs did had an impact on your action, on the HVO? How was the Serbian problem important? And you claim that this was understated, if at all, by the Prosecution in their pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, I would spend two or three minutes on that topic. Unfortunately, there is not a single war which does not result in horrific consequences, in terms of violations of international law and the international laws of war, including this. The greater the chaos, the worse things take place on the ground. Those who happened to be there are faced with an enormous problem of dealing with it. The Serb and JNA aggression, resulting in hundreds of thousands of those expelled, killed, when cities were bombed, created a crazed nation or people who lost their moral ground. Things happened which are natural to such chaos. Those who happened to be in that situation sometimes cannot control that chaos. But unless they did something wrong themselves, they should not be blamed. Irrespective of how hard someone tries, there are 8.000 killed in traffic accidents in France, or so-and-so many people are killed in factories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm sorry, I must interrupt you. I think it's absolutely improper to make such a comparison. We are talking here about war crimes, and they have nothing to do with traffic accidents. Next, you will also talk about the Mexican flu and whatnot. Please stay with what we are called to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, my question was very specific. This is your defence, as you present it, your case. I told you what the Prosecution's case was, and now, because I want to be absolutely impartial, I'm presenting your case. And your case is, among other things, that the Serbs did play a part; hence my question. What was their part which may have had all the consequences? Without going into generalities, tell us how the Serbs' actions may have impacted on the Muslims and on the Croats.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Catastrophically in any regard; socially speaking, psychologically speaking, economically speaking, ethnically speaking, morally speaking, any which way you put it. When there are 700.000 or 800.000 refugees in a country of 4 million, when there are so many killed and wounded, let's say in Mostar, then production of chaos begins, and all civilised norms are done with, so that even the most powerful individuals can no longer control them. The consequence of that cannot be transferred onto my back, because I was unable to control it all. My defence is very simple.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of the sentence. It was incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Someone should tell you, Mr. Praljak, at one point the interpreters intervened to say that they had not understood you, and that was after you had said, "My defence is very simple." So you should continue from there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My defence is very simple. If one goes through all the reasons, that I'm not going to repeat now, resulting in the situation as it was in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then there is a breakdown of everything, including what we call a civilised way of living, respecting each other. My defence is such -- is that I put all of my knowledge, effort, and ability at any point in time and anywhere, resulting in important consequences in the effort to reduce such results of chaos. As for the fact that it may not have been enough, I would like to see what someone else would have done otherwise and in which way. If it is stated that I'm guilty, then such a person should put to me what he or she would have done in my place. This is all I'm asking for in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your counsels' submissions, you said that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina boycotted the referendum. In your view, the fact that they boycotted the referendum, did it have any consequences? If so, which were they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequence was that of a complete malfunctioning of that state. They boycotted the referendum, they organised their own government, and took over 70 per cent of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian territory, militarily speaking. By this, they rendered that state inexistent in reality; it only existed on paper. Hundreds of thousands were driven from homes. Sarajevo was under siege, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact that one of the three components -- we know that we have the Serbs, the Croats, and Muslims as constituent peoples. The fact that one of them did not participate in the referendum, could that sort of anticipate or forecast problems?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Antonetti, there were indications for years prior to that, clear to anyone who reflected on the situation in Yugoslavia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina separately. There were dozens upon dozens of such indications. This one was crystal clear. This was a political position of the Serbs, who said, We do not wish that state to be the way others would like to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you, without going into detail, tell me -- I mean, this has been written. It was said that the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the JNA, attacked in 1991, not so much in 1992. Could you give me a date? When did it start, where did it start? Be brief, please, without detail. I just want to have the backdrop.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, they came to Mostar, started causing trouble. In 1992, they bombed, killing civilians in Mostar, Grude, Posusje, Siroki Brijeg, Ljubusko, as well as in Bijeljina, Foca, Ravno in 1991, in Uniste before that. It is on the border towards Knin, where they killed and expelled the population without anyone as much as raising a finger. And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still with your submissions, just as I referred earlier on to the Prosecution's submissions. In your submissions, you stated that the HZ-HB and the HVO were set up with a defensive purpose in mind. Can you be more clear about this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, if you didn't want to be expelled or killed, the way we had already witnessed in Croatia, in Vukovar, in Ilok, Dubrovnik, wherever, you had to offer resistance. This is both a right and a duty, to do so, and this duty and this right made some people organise municipalities and to defend themselves against force. This is a duty of a human being, of every citizen, and this is why HZ-HB came into being, as a means of defence. And it managed to defend both itself and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I took part in it in 1992, with good results, and I'm proud of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your written submissions, you say that it was out of need. I insist on this word "need." It is out of need that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina set up the HVO and a civilian executive government of the HVO. According to you, these were to be temporary structures, and they were supposed to operate as a war government. Therefore, in your defence case, you are saying that all this was done out of need. Could you please expound on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The necessity was to defend ourselves, and the necessity stemmed from the fact that Alija Izetbegovic was not taking care of it at all. A few days before there was a full-on aggression in Sarajevo, he claimed this: It takes two to wage a war. So if he doesn't want to fight the other side, the Serbs wouldn't want to fight. That's nonsense. He didn't react to Uniste, he didn't react to Ravno, except to say that this not our war. Well, you see, it was my war. Burning down the village of Ravno and killing people there, that was Praljak's war. It may not have been Izetbegovic's war, but it was Slobodan Praljak's war. And everything was supposed to be interim, temporary, just as it is indicated in all the documents, until the whole story was brought to its conclusion by some kind of an international agreement and peace. We, or at least some of us, were hoping that the great powers would pursue a principled policy that would put an end to it all. Unfortunately, this did not happen before 1995, and again it was done in a way that was not just. It resulted in peace, but it did not result in justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Given this, you state the following: The Croats got organised and armed themselves in order to defend themselves from the attacks made by the JNA and the Bosnian Serbs, before the Muslims actually did the same. So you are actually saying that you got organised first, you, the Croats. So could you give us some examples of this and some facts regarding this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. In the areas where I was, it was clearer, Mostar, Capljina, Bugojno, Kupres, Livno, because Croats had already seen what had happened to them in Croatia. Well, it was quite simple. You don't have to be smart. All you need to do is just watch the TV and see how your people are being killed and expelled, and you understand that this is going to happen to you, too. And it's as clear as day. But what Croats organised, they did organise it, but Muslims took part in it to an extent that they wanted. They joined the HVO units without any problems, in other words. We did not make Croat units. We organised the defence of some areas, involving all the Muslims that had signed up and all those who wanted to fight. That's my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying -- and this might be interesting, you're saying that the forces under Muslim control in Bosnia-Herzegovina were only consolidated around the end of -- between the end of the summer and the winter of 1992, end of the summer and winter of 1992. What can you say on the way the Muslim forces were actually set up?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim forces had already been organised in the format of the Patriotic League. Well, formally, there was a large number of people who had signed up, but their leadership was convincing them that there would be no war. And this resulted in the fact that the idea that the war was on their door-step was hard to grasp by some Muslims. The more Serbs attacked, the more atrocities they committed in Bijeljina and Brcko, the more Muslims joined the BH Army. The army grew in strength, in proportion to what was happening in Sarajevo, in Bihac, and so on. So, Your Honours, they simply -- in mental terms, they lagged behind Croats; not because we were smarter, but because all this had happened to us before. And they were convinced, because Alija Izetbegovic had convinced them, that the Yugoslav People's Army would be the guardian of peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for God's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also say, as far as the founding text of HZ-HB are concerned - we know we've been through this - notably the decision made on November 18, 1991, on the creation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and so forth and so on, you're saying the following, and I quote: According to you, this text shows how worried the Croatian Community was in 1991. This is a text that dates back to November 1991. So they were worried for the following reasons: Izetbegovic could very well choose to be part of a Serb-dominated Yugoslavia. So if I understand you correctly, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were afraid that Izetbegovic choose the Serbs and end up being part of a Serb-dominated Yugoslavia. And as a reaction to this, if I understood you right, there was a decision to set up the Herceg-Bosna Croatian Community. Is this the way it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let's look at this from the point of view of pure -- of simple math. Uniste was the centre of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was occupied in the summer of 1991. The Bosnian leadership -- or, rather, it was annexed by Knin. The Bosnia and Herzegovina leadership keeps silent. B, the captured Croatian soldiers from Kostajnica were given over to Serbs to put in their camps. Nobody says a word. C, the attack on Ravno happens on two occasions. The things that they did not tear down and the people that they didn't kill on the first occasion, they did that on the second time, and Izetbegovic says, This is not our war because there are only Croats living in Ravno. D, he's making a historical agreement with Milosevic. Well, I spoke about it. Well, what are we supposed to think, and what are we supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now deal with another issue, something that is contrary to the Prosecution's case, but it is an issue that you expound on. According to you, Croats never attacked the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to you, it's the ABiH who attacked Konjic and Klic [as interpreted] in March 1993, before the combat in Ahmici and Sovici. You also add that in June 1993, they attacked the Croatian village of Bijelo Polje. And, finally, you say that the HVO had reasons to believe that the ABiH's strategy was directed towards occupying part of the coast of the Republic of Croatia on the Adriatic Sea. And you also add that this was confirmed in September 1993, when the ABiH launched its Neretva-1993 offensive. To sum things up, your case is in complete contradiction with the Prosecution's case. You say that it's the ABiH who attacked first and that their main objective was to reach the Adriatic coast. You said this over and over again, of course. But could you, as briefly as possible, tell us about your case, about this case? This will also -- of course, this will be noted on the record.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina attacked in Travnik. It was the first to do so, and it emptied Travnik of Croats. The Army of B and H attacked in Konjic and emptied it of Croats and the HVO. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in April, drafted plans to attack the western part of Mostar. On the 9th of May, it attempted to carry it out. The Army of B and H, on the 30th of June, 1993, attacked HVO forces in the Northern Camp and in Bijelo Polje, and their members within the HVO ranks rebelled with arms against their own armed force, killing and capturing many Croats. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina attacked Bugojno and emptied it of all Croats. The Army of B and H initiated an offensive at Bugojno which went on until they realised they would never capture a part of the coast that does not belong to them. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina attacked along the front-line of 200 kilometres for several months. The Army of B and H, together with the Muslim leadership, arranged with the Serb side a peace or a truce in September and a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are all facts that cannot be disputed. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina attacked Vares, driving away the Croats, and so on and so forth. If the Prosecutor has any proof, any evidence on the attacks and offensive operations of the HVO, I would kindly ask them to put them to the Tribunal, except for the tactical movements resulting in regaining lost territory and the movements -- slight movements of the lines. If they have anything to that effect, let them show us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: General Praljak, I only would like to ask you, I wonder if you may provide us with some dates when you mention those events? I believe it would be very helpful for us and for everyone if you could add that. Of course, now I know that you may not be prepared to give us the exact dates as of now, but at least to try to do so in order to give us more facts as far as the -- as far as what happened there and as far as the attacks occurred, in your view, before any other steps which were undertaken by the HVO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Konjic, the attack started in late March 1993. In Travnik, the attacks started in June 1993, in early June 1993. In Bugojno -- well, first in Mostar. In Mostar, the preparations for an attack and orders are issued in April 1993. The attack was carried out on the 9th of May, 1993. On the 30th of June, 1993, they attacked Northern Camp, where the HVO units were stationed. Bijelo Polje, in Stolac, they committed murder. They disarmed wherever they could. HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnic background disarmed HVO soldiers of Croatian ethnic background, in accordance with the previous instructions they received from the 4th Corps. The attack on Bugojno started sometime in mid-July 1993, and it continues on with the attack on Vakuf. And those attacks continue into 1994, with greater or smaller intensity. What they refer to as the offensive in 1993 was launched in September 1993, and Muslim commanders wrote what they wrote about it. I have nothing to add to their words. It's just a continuation of an offensive that had already started in Central Bosnia a long time ago, an offensive on Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Novi Travnik. And then it continues on with some cease-fire agreements that were signed, that they violated up until the time when the Washington Agreement was signed. In Vares, they attacked four or five days before the 23rd. Before Stupni Do, the attacks had already started by the 3rd Corps. There are orders issued by them to that effect, and I quoted from a book written by the general who was in charge of the operation, General Alagic. The balance of powers in Central Bosnia, between the HVO units and the two corps of the BH Army, was such, and those people were encircled. It was more than 10:1. Now I leave you in peace to decide whether any commander, even if they wanted to, with no logistics support - it was possible to resupply the units only by helicopter - how can a commander launch any offensive against the enemy that outnumbers him 10:1. We were defending ourselves, we were barely holding on, and all this, in political and military sense, was defined by the agreement with Serbs in September 1993, the political and military agreement, what they wanted. Fortunately, we were not as weak as all that, and we managed to hold on, albeit with great casualties and efforts. I was the commander of the Main Staff, and I don't have any criticism to levy against myself, my lads, my subordinate commanders. We managed to defend ourselves. So that's my answer to you, Your Honour Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this ratio of 10:1 leads me to my last question, because we're almost finished for the day. In your written submission, you say something that has already been stated, but I'll remind you. You say that if the Croats had really wanted to attack the Muslim Bosnians, they would have done so in the summer or the fall of 1992, when the Croats were at the very top -- at the very height and apex of their military power, compared to the Muslims in Bosnia. So you say that if you had been the attack -- if you had been the ones who attacked, you would have done so before 1992, before they were actually setting up their forces. Could you please expound on this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. If I had had -- and I'm not as stupid as all that so that you cannot understand me. So had there been a plan that I was supposed to implement, in 1992 I would not have distributed more rifles to the Muslims than to Croats. We would not have, after the liberation of Stolac, when there were no Muslims there, returned all the Muslims who wished to return to that town, trained and set up their brigades, armed them, kept on supplying weapons and ammunition to them throughout the war. For God's sake, this is what I'm saying, loud and clear, in 1992, had there been any plan because of all those things. So I could have disarmed every Muslim in Mostar, and I could have captured Vakuf, Rama, and all that, instead of fighting all those morons up there, getting their rifles, and returning 75 per cent of the Muslims to their homes. We did not want to fight the war against Muslims, not at that time or ever. All the transcripts, all the speeches, they all referred to the defence and the survival of Croats, and the 17.5 per cent of the possible territory that Croats should have some kind of a self-administration or self-government over. That's the minimum solution, and that was the policy -- that was the position of all of us, and this is how we acted. This is how we treated the wounded, the refugees, the population, the medicines, weapons. I simply cannot understand how somebody could draft an indictment like this. I simply cannot understand it. You have thousands of documents that speak to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's another problem. But it's now 7.00 p.m. We will stop for the day. Tomorrow, General Praljak, I'll ask you my final questions on your defence case, on your defence strategy, so please keep all this for tomorrow. You'll have time to talk about this tomorrow. But tomorrow, I will talk about the submissions of April. There's about 50 documents. I will say what you wrote -- I will say, You wrote this in your pre-trial brief, this is -- or in your submission, this is the document that backs it, and could you please comment on this. I've prepared this for quite a while, so I will immediately go to the crux of the matter. So I invite all the other counsels of Defence to also get ready for their own cross-examination. I don't know who's going to start. I'm sure there will be also questions from my fellow Judges. But once my fellow Judges are done with their questions, the Defence will have to be ready for cross-examining Mr. Praljak. You can sleep over this, of course. This week, we're sitting in the morning, so we will resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. Have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
